lesson.title: Wide or Narrow: What Controls a Confidence Interval's Width
lesson.summary: A confidence interval's width is set entirely by its margin of error, which grows with a higher confidence level and shrinks with a larger sample size or less variable data.
lesson.body:
A confidence interval's width is simply twice its margin of error, and the margin of error is z star times the standard error, sqrt(p-hat(1-p-hat)/n). That one formula reveals every lever available for controlling how wide or narrow an interval turns out to be: the confidence level, through z star, the sample size n, and the variability of the outcome itself, through p-hat(1-p-hat).

Raising the confidence level increases z star, which widens the interval, because demanding more certainty that the interval captures the true parameter requires casting a wider net. Using the voter survey data again, p-hat = 0.55 and n = 400, so the standard error is about 0.0249 regardless of confidence level. At 90 percent confidence, z star is 1.645, giving a margin of error of about 1.645 times 0.0249, which is about 0.0409. At 95 percent confidence, z star is 1.96, giving a margin of error of about 0.0488, as computed earlier. At 99 percent confidence, z star is 2.576, giving a margin of error of about 2.576 times 0.0249, which is about 0.0641. The resulting widths are about 0.082 at 90 percent, 0.098 at 95 percent, and 0.128 at 99 percent, confirming that more confidence always costs a wider interval when nothing else changes.

Sample size works the opposite direction. Because the standard error involves dividing by n inside a square root, quadrupling the sample size cuts the standard error in half, not to a quarter, since the square root softens the effect. If the same survey had polled 1600 voters instead of 400, four times as many, and found the same 55 percent support, the standard error would be sqrt(0.2475/1600), which is exactly half of sqrt(0.2475/400), about 0.0124 instead of 0.0249. Half the standard error means half the margin of error at any fixed confidence level, and therefore a noticeably narrower interval. This is why serious polls and studies invest in large samples, more data buys precision, but only at the reduced rate governed by the square root.

The third factor, p-hat(1-p-hat), is largest when p-hat is close to 0.5 and shrinks as p-hat moves toward 0 or 1, since a proportion near an extreme has less room to vary. A survey where almost everyone agrees, say p-hat = 0.95, will naturally produce a narrower interval than one where opinion is split down the middle, even with the same sample size and confidence level, simply because there is less underlying variability to estimate. Taken together, these three factors set up the natural next question: if you need an interval no wider than some target margin of error, how large a sample do you need to guarantee it? That is the subject of the next chapter.
